popular_table.note: A lapse rate is a description of a layer of air at a moment, not a law. It changes by the hour, which is why deriving it from two live measurements beats remembering it.

faq: How do I calculate a lapse rate from two stations?
Rate = (lower temperature − upper temperature) ÷ (upper elevation − lower elevation), scaled to per-kilometre. A 13°C difference over 2 km is 6.5°C/km.
A layer cooling faster than 9.8°C/km — unstable, usually thin and near sun-heated ground. Air in it overturns eagerly; thermals and dust devils are its signature.
Does the lapse rate change with season?
Yes — the environmental rate varies with weather, season and place. The 6.5 figure is a standardised average for the troposphere, useful exactly because real rates scatter around it.
Why do pilots care about the dry rate specifically?

A rising parcel of unsaturated air cools at the dry adiabatic rate regardless of the environment. Comparing parcel and environment rates predicts whether the parcel keeps rising — stability in one subtraction.
Can the calculator handle Fahrenheit and feet?
Yes — rates convert consistently (9.8°C/km equals about 5.4°F per 1,000 ft). Mixing units inside one calculation is the error to avoid.
The standard lapse applies through the troposphere; above the tropopause temperature stops falling and the model ends. For surface-to-summit work on Earth, you are always inside the troposphere.
How does this relate to boiling point and pressure?
All three ride the same thinning air: temperature by lapse, pressure by the barometric formula, boiling point by pressure. The sibling tools on this site compute each from elevation.
